body:
Why the colonial government required civil servants

A large territorial administration needed officials who could collect revenue, maintain records, supervise districts, prepare reports and implement government orders. These officials formed the civil service: the permanent administrative staff of the state, as distinct from its soldiers.

Senior civil servants were especially influential because they connected the government of a Presidency or province with local district administration. Their work affected revenue demands, the implementation of regulations and the exercise of executive authority.

Company patronage and the covenanted service

In the Company's earlier system, appointments to the senior service depended heavily on patronage. The Company's Court of Directors nominated candidates, who received training before being sent to India. Haileybury College in Britain became an important training institution.

Patronage

Patronage means obtaining an appointment through nomination or the influence of a person holding authority, rather than through an open competition in which eligible candidates are assessed under common examination rules.

The higher service was known as the covenanted civil service because its members entered into formal service agreements with the Company. Lower administrative positions were often filled through the uncovenanted service, in which many Indians were employed. The distinction concerned recruitment arrangements, service conditions and access to senior posts.

Cornwallis and the senior services

Lord Cornwallis, Governor-General during important reforms of the late 18th century, sought to make the Company's administration more regular and less dependent on private gain. Higher salaries, prescribed official duties and restrictions on private trading were intended to discourage corruption among senior officials.

These reforms also reinforced European dominance in the highest offices. Indians continued to perform essential work in subordinate and local administration, but their opportunities to enter the senior covenanted service remained severely restricted.

From nomination to competitive examination

The Charter Act of 1833 declared through Section 87 that specified differences of religion, birthplace, descent or colour should not by themselves disqualify a person from Company employment. This legal statement did not immediately establish an effective competitive system.

The decisive recruitment change came through the Charter Act of 1853, which provided for competitive selection. The Macaulay Committee's report of 1854 shaped the new method, and the first competitive Indian Civil Service examinations were held in London in 1855.

The examinations replaced directors' nomination as the normal route into the higher civil service. However, competition did not automatically mean equal opportunity. Candidates had to travel to Britain, sit examinations in English and prepare for a syllabus that gave considerable weight to European classical subjects. Age restrictions also placed Indian candidates at a disadvantage.

First Indian entry into the Indian Civil Service

Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian to enter the Indian Civil Service through the competitive examination system. He passed the examination in 1863 and joined the service in 1864. He subsequently served in the Bombay Presidency.

His entry was an important exception to a system still dominated by Europeans. It did not immediately remove the practical disadvantages facing Indian candidates.

Separate the recruitment milestones

1853 provided for competitive selection; 1854 brought the Macaulay Committee report; 1855 saw the first London examination; 1863 was the year Satyendranath Tagore passed; and 1864 was the year he joined the service.

Prelims focus

  • Covenanted civil service: higher Company service entered through formal agreements.
  • Uncovenanted service: important source of subordinate administrative appointments.
  • 1853: Charter Act provided for competitive civil-service recruitment.
  • 1854: Macaulay Committee report.
  • 1855: first competitive Indian Civil Service examination in London.
  • Satyendranath Tagore: first Indian to pass, in 1863; joined in 1864.
  • Trap: Competitive examinations began before direct Crown rule in 1858.

[Union Public Service Commission, About Us, section Historical Perspective, consulted 20 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, UPSC: A Century of Meritocracy and Inclusion, 30 September 2026, section The Road to 1926; Government of India Act 1833, Section 87, original enacted text; P. J. Griffiths, The British Impact on India, discussion of Cornwallis and the covenanted civil service.]

pictures.alt: Timeline separates the 1853 Act, 1854 report, 1855 London examination, and Satyendranath Tagore passing in 1863 and joining in 1864.
pictures.caption: The move to competitive recruitment occurred through several separate steps.

title: Colonial Civil Service: Recruitment, Reform and Indian Entry

body:
Why the district became the working unit of government

The colonial government could issue regulations from Calcutta or another Presidency centre, but those decisions had to be implemented in villages, towns and agricultural areas. The district became the main unit through which officials carried out revenue administration and coordinated other government functions.

District administration connected central or provincial authority with local people. Its central tasks were to assess and collect revenue, maintain records, implement government orders and support the maintenance of public order.

The Collector and revenue administration

The title Collector came from the official's principal responsibility for collecting government revenue. Land revenue was especially important to Company finances. The Collector supervised records of revenue obligations, payments and arrears, and worked through subordinate officials who dealt directly with landholders and villages.

The district office was commonly known as the Collectorate. It became an important centre for official correspondence, revenue records and the implementation of administrative orders.

Revenue administration was not identical to the administration of justice. A dispute about a revenue payment, for example, could involve both the collection machinery and a court empowered to determine legal rights. The authority to demand payment and the authority to decide a legal dispute were conceptually different functions, even when early Company arrangements placed several powers in the same official's hands.

Collector and Magistrate: offices and functions

A Magistrate exercised powers connected with criminal administration and the maintenance of public order. A District Judge exercised judicial authority in the district's courts. The Collector was primarily a revenue administrator, although executive and magisterial duties were combined with the Collector's office in many later district arrangements.

These relationships changed over time. Under Warren Hastings's early arrangements, Company district officials combined or supervised several administrative and judicial responsibilities. In Bengal, the Cornwallis Code of 1793 attempted a clearer separation: the Collector was confined chiefly to revenue administration, while judicial and certain magisterial responsibilities were assigned to district judges.

That separation was subsequently modified. In many provinces, the district's principal executive official came to hold the combined designation Collector and District Magistrate, while a separate judicial establishment handled regular civil and criminal trials.

A changing arrangement, not an unchanging rule

It is inaccurate to assume that the Collector possessed exactly the same judicial and magisterial powers throughout British rule. The division of functions changed with reforms and differed across provinces.

How district offices were connected

Under the mature colonial arrangement, the Collector or District Magistrate coordinated district executive administration. Subordinate revenue officials handled smaller territorial units. Police officers investigated offences and maintained public order under their own chain of command, subject to the district magistrate's general supervisory authority where provided by law. Courts decided legal disputes through judicial officers.

Gujarat connection: Kaira and Ahmedabad

Colonial district administration developed in the Gujarat territories brought under direct British control. The historical name Kaira corresponds to Kheda.

After territorial acquisitions in Gujarat in the early 19th century, a Collector was appointed in 1805 to administer ceded territories around Kaira and neighbouring areas. Following further acquisitions, the territory north of the Mahi River was divided into the separate districts of Kaira and Ahmedabad from 1 January 1818.

These districts belonged to the British administrative system associated with the Bombay Presidency. They illustrate how the collectorate became a practical institution as British-controlled territory expanded. This did not mean that the whole of present-day Gujarat was directly administered in the same way: princely states such as Baroda retained distinct political arrangements under British paramountcy.

Prelims focus

  • Collector: principal district revenue officer.
  • Collectorate: the district's administrative and revenue office.
  • District Magistrate: executive authority associated with maintaining public order.
  • District Judge: judicial authority, distinct from the Collector's revenue functions.
  • 1793: Cornwallis reforms separated revenue collection from judicial functions in Bengal.
  • 1805: Collector appointed for ceded territories around Kaira.
  • 1 January 1818: Kaira and Ahmedabad organised as separate districts.
  • Trap: The Collector's combination of revenue, magisterial and judicial functions changed across periods.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, section Setting up a New Administration, printed pp. 21–22, 2020–21 printing; P. J. Griffiths, The British Impact on India, discussion of district administration and the Cornwallis reforms of 1793; W. W. Hunter, Imperial Gazetteer of India, 2nd edition, 1886, Volume VII, entry Kaira, printed pp. 300–301 and 307.]

pictures.alt: Revenue and public order often shared a Collector–District Magistrate, while the District Judge and courts handled judicial functions.
pictures.caption: Revenue collection, public order and judicial decisions were distinct functions within district administration.

title: District Administration: Collector, Magistrate and Local Government

body:
Why the British reorganised policing

Territorial government required a means of preventing crime, arresting suspects, maintaining public order and enforcing lawful administrative directions. The Company's early police arrangements were not uniform across India. They drew partly on existing local institutions, including village watchmen and the responsibilities previously exercised by landholders and local authorities.

As the Company expanded its territorial control, its administrators sought a more regular system that would answer to government officials rather than depend entirely on local landholders.

Cornwallis and the daroga system

Under reforms associated with Lord Cornwallis in Bengal during the early 1790s, policing was brought more directly under government supervision. Districts were divided into police areas called thanas, with a daroga placed in charge of each thana.

Thana and daroga

A thana was a local police jurisdiction or station. A daroga was the officer responsible for policing that area under the colonial arrangements.

The system reduced the formal police responsibilities of zamindars in areas where the reforms were introduced. Darogas and their subordinates worked under the supervision of magistrates and other government authorities.

The new arrangement created clearer lines of official control, but it did not solve every problem. Limited resources, misconduct and difficulties in preventing crime continued to affect colonial policing.

Reorganisation after 1857

Following the uprising of 1857 and the transfer to Crown rule, the British government sought to reorganise policing on a more systematic basis. A Police Commission was appointed in 1860, and the Police Act of 1861 provided a framework for organised police forces.

The Police Act of 1861 was enacted on 22 March 1861. Its stated purpose was to reorganise the police and improve the prevention and detection of crime.

Structure under the Police Act of 1861

The Act's principal arrangements included:

  • Section 2: the police establishment within the relevant administrative jurisdiction was to constitute an organised police force.
  • Section 3: overall supervision of the police was vested in the government responsible for that jurisdiction.
  • Section 4: an Inspector-General of Police headed the wider police administration, while the District Superintendent of Police managed district police under the general control and direction of the district magistrate.

Police and magistracy were not the same institution

The Superintendent of Police headed police operations within the district. The District Magistrate exercised general control and direction where the applicable legal arrangements provided for it. Thus, the police had its own organisational hierarchy while remaining connected to the district executive.

The police investigated offences and maintained public order; courts determined guilt and imposed sentences according to the applicable law. The power to arrest a suspect did not itself make a police officer a trial judge.

The Police Act of 1861 did not automatically bring every province and Presidency town under an identical police system on the same date. Its application and the relevant police laws varied across British India.

The colonial police served ordinary law-enforcement functions but also protected the authority of the colonial government. These purposes sometimes overlapped, particularly when officials viewed public gatherings or resistance to government orders as threats to order.

Prelims focus

  • Cornwallis: associated with the daroga and thana system in Bengal during the early 1790s.
  • Daroga: officer in charge of a thana.
  • 1860: Police Commission appointed.
  • 22 March 1861: Police Act enacted.
  • Section 4: Inspector-General and District Superintendent of Police.
  • District Magistrate: general control and direction of district police under the Act's framework.
  • Trap: The District Superintendent of Police and the District Magistrate were different offices.

[India Code, Police Act 1861, Act 5 of 1861, preamble and Sections 2–4, official statutory text, consulted 20 November 2026; A. Kumara Swamy, Community Policing in Andhra Pradesh: A Case Study of Hyderabad Police, Osmania University, 2018, Chapter 2, sections 2.4–2.4.2, printed pp. 106–108, hosted by the Bureau of Police Research and Development; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, printed pp. 21–22, 2020–21 printing.]

pictures.alt: Government supervises the police hierarchy; the District Magistrate separately exercises general control and direction over district police.
pictures.caption: The Act distinguished the police chain of command from the magistrate's general district control.

title: Colonial Police: From the Daroga System to the Police Act of 1861
